title: Asymmetric Textured Image Sensors Based on Antenna Theory as Designed by Nature
abstract: This work numerically validates the application of bio-inspired concepts on CMOS derived from bacterial photosynthetic light harvesters. We investigate a modification of symmetric inverted pyramid array CMOS image sensors into an asymmetrically shaped texture to explore the structural boundary of passive non-reciprocity. Diverging from traditional macroscopic continuum assumptions, we analyze whether structural asymmetry at sub-wavelength scales can induce non-reciprocal scattering under passive, linear, and time-invariant conditions. A theoretical framework based on perturbation theory is developed, estimating a potential efficiency enhancement of 5\% to 15\%. Numerical simulations performed via the MEEP finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) platform reveal that the linear response is highly localized, showing a subtle 0.02\% change. This suggests that macroscopic Lorentz reciprocity remains robust at the investigated scale due to apex field concentration, defining a clear geometric threshold for microscopic non-reciprocity.
summary: This paper explores inducing passive non-reciprocal scattering in textured image sensors by introducing structural asymmetry at sub-wavelength scales. Using antenna theory and FDTD simulations, the authors find that while theory predicts significant enhancement, actual measurements show this effect is suppressed by field concentration at sharp apices. Future designs must focus on asymmetric modifications directly at these high-field regions.
main_problem: The work investigates whether structural asymmetry at sub-wavelength scales can induce passive non-reciprocal scattering in linear, time-invariant systems, moving beyond traditional macroscopic continuum assumptions.
main_result: While theory predicts a potential 5%-15% efficiency enhancement via symmetry breaking, numerical simulations reveal that intense local field concentration at the apex shields this effect, suggesting asymmetry must be engineered directly at the field-concentrating point to observe non-reciprocity.
method: The study combines theoretical development using perturbation theory with detailed numerical simulations performed on the MEEP finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) platform.
model_or_system: The physical system is a CMOS image sensor modified with an asymmetrically textured surface, inspired by bacterial photosynthetic light harvesters. The model analyzes wave scattering properties at the sub-wavelength scale using antenna theory principles.

main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that macroscopic continuum models are invalid at the sub-wavelength scale, and that geometric configuration dictates the electromagnetic response.

paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical framework based on bio-inspiration and perturbation theory, through numerical validation using MEEP/FDTD simulations comparing various geometries (circular vs. elliptical), culminating in a discussion of the discrepancy between predicted enhancement and measured results.
why_interesting: Although focused on classical optics/photonics, the investigation into symmetry breaking to induce non-reciprocity at nanoscale boundaries touches upon concepts relevant to topological photonics or engineered quantum light-matter interactions where boundary conditions are paramount.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The geometry used in MEEP Project 4 for calculating the CMOS image sensor [20]. A silicon dioxide glass microlens with a 0.85µm radius of curvature is atop the image sensor to focus incident light into individual pixels. Surrounding each pixel is a metal aperture grid composed of tungsten wire (0.1µm wide and 0.2µm high), which sits on a 3 µm thick crystalline-silicon substrate. Furthermore, deep-trench isolation-implemented as a 0.1µm wide and 2µm thick silicon-dioxide trench-surrounds the pixel to mitigate electrical crosstalk and trap photons via index guiding.

FIG. 2. According to experimental data, the major axis of Rhodopseudomonas palustris has length 110 ˚A and the minor axis is 95 ˚A; the largest dimension of the inner LH1 is 78 ˚A [22]. The elliptical symmetry is visualized by superimposing our model onto the schematic representation based on X-ray data.

FIG. 3. (a)-(b) Original circular cone from MEEP project 4, (c)-(d) modified circular cone, and (e)-(f) proposed asymmetric elliptical cone. For all subfigures, the horizontal (X) axis represents the optical wavelength ranging from 0.7 to 1.0 µm. The vertical (Y) axis represents the absolute coefficient value (absorption and reflection) for the left column [subfigures (a), (c), (e)] and the relative enhancement factor for the right column [subfigures (b), (d), (f)].
FIG. 4. Calculated silicon substrate optical absorption curves under oblique incident illumination (θ = 0◦, 15◦, 30◦) for the asymmetric elliptical base cone texture array.
